overview: Repartition is a Spark transformation that redistributes data across a specified number of partitions by triggering a full shuffle of the data over the network.
It can both increase or decrease the number of partitions, and can hash-partition data by one or more columns to co-locate related rows.
Because it performs a full shuffle, repartition is the primary tool for fixing data skew and creating evenly-sized partitions, but it is expensive.
learningObjectives: Understand how repartition(n) and repartition(col) redistribute data and why a full shuffle is involved.
Learn to use repartition to fix skewed or undersized partitions and to control parallelism.
Distinguish repartition from coalesce and know when the shuffle cost is justified.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: repartition is a wide transformation on a Spark DataFrame/RDD that returns a new dataset with exactly the requested number of partitions, redistributing all rows through a full shuffle. When given column arguments, it applies hash partitioning so that all rows sharing the same key land in the same partition; when given only a number, it round-robin distributes rows to produce evenly-sized partitions.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine your data is split into uneven piles, some huge and some tiny. repartition takes all the data, throws it into the air, and re-deals it into a chosen number of equal piles. If you tell it to deal by a column (like customer_id), every card with the same value ends up in the same pile. This re-dealing is thorough and fair, but moving all the cards around takes real effort.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Repartition has existed since the early RDD API of Apache Spark (repartition was added in Spark 1.0 as a wrapper over coalesce with shuffle=true). With the introduction of DataFrames and Catalyst, repartition(numPartitions, *cols) gained hash-partitioning semantics. Adaptive Query Execution (AQE), introduced in Spark 3.0, automated some repartitioning decisions like coalescing shuffle partitions, reducing the need for manual repartition tuning in many pipelines.

whyItMatters.business: Properly repartitioned data prevents straggler tasks that delay job completion, ensuring SLAs are met for reports, dashboards, and downstream consumers. Balanced partitions reduce wall-clock runtime and cluster cost.
whyItMatters.engineering: Repartition gives engineers explicit control over parallelism and data layout, enabling them to eliminate skew, match partition counts to cluster cores, and pre-partition data by join keys to reduce later shuffles.
whyItMatters.scalability: As data volumes grow, partition counts must scale to keep each task's memory footprint manageable. Repartition lets pipelines increase parallelism so that no single executor is overwhelmed by an oversized partition.
whyItMatters.cost: Skewed partitions cause a few tasks to run long while the rest of the cluster sits idle, wasting paid compute. Repartition trades a one-time shuffle cost for far better cluster utilization, often lowering total cost.
whyItMatters.reliability: Oversized partitions are the leading cause of executor OutOfMemory errors and spills. Repartition reduces per-partition size, making jobs more stable and less likely to fail under load.

coreComponents.name: Shuffle Mechanism
coreComponents.definition: The network-wide data movement that repartition triggers, writing map-side output to disk and reading it on the reduce side.
coreComponents.purpose: To physically relocate rows so that the new partitioning scheme (round-robin or hash) is satisfied across executors.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Serialize, write shuffle files, transfer over the network, and re-read data; this is the dominant cost of repartition.
coreComponents.examples: A shuffle stage boundary appearing in the Spark UI DAG after a repartition call.

coreComponents.name: Partitioner (HashPartitioner / RoundRobin)
coreComponents.definition: The logic that decides which target partition each row goes to.
coreComponents.purpose: repartition(col) uses a HashPartitioner on the column hash; repartition(n) uses round-robin to evenly spread rows.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Compute target partition = hash(key) % numPartitions for column-based, or rotate assignments for numeric-only repartition.
coreComponents.examples: df.repartition(200, "customer_id") groups all rows of a customer into one partition via hashing.

coreComponents.name: Target Partition Count (numPartitions)
coreComponents.definition: The exact number of output partitions the resulting dataset will have.
coreComponents.purpose: To set the degree of parallelism for downstream stages and control per-partition data size.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Guarantee that the output has precisely numPartitions partitions, even if it means creating empty ones.
coreComponents.examples: Setting numPartitions to a multiple of total executor cores (e.g., 2x-3x) for good utilization.

internalWorking: When repartition is called, Spark inserts a shuffle (exchange) operator into the physical plan, creating a stage boundary at that point.

In the map phase, each existing partition's rows are assigned to target partitions using the chosen partitioner (round-robin for repartition(n), hash for repartition(col)), and the results are written to local shuffle files bucketed by target partition.

In the reduce phase, each new task fetches its bucket from every map output across the cluster over the network, assembling exactly numPartitions partitions, after which downstream transformations run on the rebalanced data.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Input Partitions (uneven) -> Map-side Partitioner (hash or round-robin) -> Shuffle Write (local disk) -> Network Transfer -> Shuffle Read -> Output Partitions (exactly numPartitions, balanced)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A DataFrame is read from a source and ends up with 4 highly uneven partitions (one holds 80% of the rows).
2. df.repartition(8) is called, inserting a full shuffle stage into the plan.
3. Each of the 4 source tasks reads its rows and round-robin assigns them across 8 target buckets, writing shuffle files.
4. 8 new reduce tasks each fetch their bucket from all 4 map outputs over the network.
5. The result is 8 evenly-sized partitions, eliminating the original skew and enabling balanced parallel processing downstream.

keyTerminology.meaning: The process of redistributing data across partitions and executors over the network, involving disk writes and reads.
keyTerminology.importance: Repartition always triggers a full shuffle, which is the most expensive operation in Spark and the key cost to weigh.

keyTerminology.meaning: An uneven distribution where some partitions hold far more data than others, causing straggler tasks.
keyTerminology.importance: Repartition (especially round-robin repartition(n)) is the canonical remedy for skew.

keyTerminology.meaning: A partitioner that places rows into partition hash(key) % numPartitions.
keyTerminology.importance: Used by repartition(col) to co-locate rows with the same key, useful before joins and aggregations.

importantConcepts.explanation: repartition(n) distributes rows round-robin for maximum evenness regardless of content. repartition(n, col) hashes by the column, which co-locates same-key rows but can itself create skew if the column has skewed key distribution.

This config (default 200) controls the number of partitions produced by shuffles like joins and aggregations. repartition(n) overrides it for that specific operation by taking an explicit count, but tuning the config matters for implicit shuffles.

variationsAndTypes: **repartition(numPartitions):** Round-robin redistribution into an exact partition count; best for fixing skew and setting parallelism.
**repartition(numPartitions, *cols):** Hash partitioning by the given columns into the exact count; co-locates same-key rows.
**repartition(*cols):** Hash partitioning by columns using spark.sql.shuffle.partitions as the count; useful before key-based operations.
**repartitionByRange(numPartitions, *cols):** Range partitioning that sorts data into ranges, useful for ordered writes and range queries.
advantages: **Eliminates Skew:** Round-robin repartition produces evenly-sized partitions, removing straggler tasks.
**Increases Parallelism:** Can raise the partition count to use more cores and shrink per-partition memory.
**Key Co-location:** repartition(col) groups same-key rows together, reducing shuffles in subsequent joins/aggregations.
**Predictable Layout:** Produces exactly the requested number of partitions, giving deterministic downstream parallelism.
disadvantages: **Full Shuffle Cost:** Always moves all data over the network with disk I/O, the most expensive Spark operation.
**Memory and Disk Pressure:** Shuffle write/read can spill to disk and stress executor memory.
**Potential Hash Skew:** repartition(col) on a skewed key column reintroduces uneven partitions.
**Overhead for Small Reductions:** When only reducing partitions, repartition is wasteful compared to coalesce.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use repartition when you need to increase partitions, fix data skew with even distribution, or hash-partition by a key before repeated joins/aggregations on that key. The shuffle cost is justified when the resulting balance or co-location saves more time downstream.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid repartition when you only need to reduce the number of partitions and don't require even sizing, where coalesce avoids the shuffle. Also avoid hash-repartitioning on a heavily skewed key, which simply relocates the skew.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Think of repartition as a casino dealer collecting all the cards from uneven stacks on the table, reshuffling the entire deck, and re-dealing them into a fixed number of equal hands. If asked to deal by suit (a column), all hearts go to one player. The re-deal is fair and exact, but gathering and reshuffling every card takes time and effort, just like a full network shuffle.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Repartition and coalesce are interchangeable ways to change partition count.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Coalesce avoids a full shuffle by merging adjacent partitions and can only reduce count; repartition always shuffles and can increase or evenly redistribute. They have very different cost and balance characteristics.

commonMisconceptions.myth: More partitions from repartition always means faster jobs.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Too many tiny partitions create excessive task scheduling overhead and small shuffle files. The goal is right-sized partitions (often ~128MB each, partition count a small multiple of total cores), not simply more.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Repartition lets pipelines scale parallelism with data volume, but the shuffle it triggers scales in cost with data size; oversized shuffles can saturate network and disk, so partition counts should be tuned to cluster capacity.
productionConsiderations.reliability: By shrinking oversized partitions, repartition reduces executor OOM and spill failures, improving job stability under large or skewed inputs.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Shuffle output is materialized to disk, so on task failure Spark can re-fetch shuffle blocks; however, lost shuffle files (e.g., executor loss) can force expensive stage recomputation.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch the Spark UI for shuffle read/write sizes, task duration variance (skew), and spill metrics to confirm repartition achieved balance and to size partitions correctly.
productionConsiderations.security: Shuffle data written to local disk and transferred over the network should be encrypted (spark.io.encryption.enabled, spark.network.crypto.enabled) when handling sensitive data, since repartition materializes intermediate data.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Balancing partitions with repartition removes idle-cluster waste from stragglers, but unnecessary repartitions add shuffle cost; only repartition when downstream savings exceed the shuffle expense.
productionConsiderations.performance: Performance hinges on partition sizing (~100-200MB), avoiding too many small partitions, and using coalesce instead when merely reducing count. Enabling AQE can auto-coalesce post-shuffle partitions.

codeExamples.title: Increasing Partitions and Fixing Skew with repartition(n)
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrates inspecting partition count, then using round-robin repartition to evenly redistribute a skewed DataFrame and increase parallelism.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("RepartitionDemo").getOrCreate()

df = spark.read.parquet("/data/events")

# Inspect current number of partitions
print("Before:", df.rdd.getNumPartitions())

# Round-robin repartition into 200 evenly-sized partitions (full shuffle)
balanced = df.repartition(200)
print("After:", balanced.rdd.getNumPartitions())

# Verify even distribution by counting rows per partition
from pyspark.sql.functions import spark_partition_id, count
balanced.groupBy(spark_partition_id().alias("pid")).agg(count("*").alias("rows")).orderBy("pid").show(5)
codeExamples.breakdown: df.rdd.getNumPartitions() reports the existing layout. df.repartition(200) triggers a full shuffle and round-robin distributes rows into exactly 200 partitions. The spark_partition_id() trick counts rows per partition so you can confirm the skew is gone.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
Before: 4
After: 200
A table showing roughly equal row counts across partition ids, confirming even distribution.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Calling repartition with too high a number creates many tiny partitions and high task overhead. Forgetting that this is a wide transformation can surprise you with an unexpected shuffle stage in the UI.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Choose numPartitions as a small multiple (2x-3x) of total executor cores, targeting ~128MB per partition. Enable AQE (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true) to let Spark coalesce shuffle partitions automatically.

codeExamples.title: Hash Partitioning by Column Before a Join
codeExamples.overview: Shows repartition(n, col) to hash-partition both sides of a join by the join key, co-locating matching rows.
codeExamples.code:
# Hash-partition by customer_id so same keys land in the same partition
orders_p = orders.repartition(100, "customer_id")
customers_p = customers.repartition(100, "customer_id")

# Join on the pre-partitioned key
result = orders_p.join(customers_p, on="customer_id", how="inner")

result.explain()  # Inspect the physical plan for Exchange operators
result.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("/data/joined")
codeExamples.breakdown: repartition(100, "customer_id") applies a HashPartitioner so all rows with the same customer_id are in the same partition on both DataFrames. result.explain() reveals the Exchange (shuffle) nodes; pre-partitioning aligns the data layout for the join.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A physical plan showing Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 100) nodes, and a successfully written joined Parquet dataset.
codeExamples.commonIssues: If customer_id is skewed (a few customers dominate), hash repartitioning recreates skew in specific partitions. Spark may still re-shuffle for the join if partition counts or partitioners do not match exactly.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: For skewed keys, prefer salting or AQE skew-join handling (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled) instead of plain hash repartition. Match numPartitions on both sides to avoid an extra exchange.

codeExamples.title: repartition vs coalesce When Reducing Partitions
codeExamples.overview: Contrasts the shuffle behavior of repartition and coalesce when lowering the partition count before a write.
codeExamples.code:
# Suppose df currently has 1000 partitions

# coalesce: no full shuffle, merges adjacent partitions, may be uneven
df.coalesce(10).write.mode("overwrite").parquet("/out/coalesced")

# repartition: full shuffle, evenly-sized partitions, but expensive
df.repartition(10).write.mode("overwrite").parquet("/out/repartitioned")
codeExamples.breakdown: Both reduce 1000 partitions to 10 and produce 10 output files. coalesce(10) avoids a shuffle by merging partitions, but the 10 partitions may be uneven. repartition(10) shuffles to guarantee even partitions at the cost of moving all data.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Both write 10 Parquet files. The coalesced version completes faster (no shuffle) but may have uneven file sizes; the repartitioned version has even files but runs slower due to the shuffle.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using repartition to reduce files when coalesce would suffice wastes time on an unnecessary shuffle. Using coalesce to a very small number can collapse upstream parallelism and cause OOM in the producing stage.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Prefer coalesce for simply reducing output file count. Use repartition only when even partition sizing or higher partition count is required.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retail analytics team runs a daily aggregation over clickstream events, but the job consistently has a few tasks that take 10x longer than others, blowing past the morning SLA. Investigation shows the input data is heavily skewed across partitions, leaving most of the cluster idle while a handful of tasks struggle.
endToEndExample.inputData: A 500GB Parquet dataset of clickstream events read into roughly 12 highly uneven partitions, where one partition holds nearly half the data due to how the upstream system wrote files.
endToEndExample.architecture: A Spark job on a cluster of 20 executors (4 cores each, 80 total cores) reads the Parquet events, repartitions for balance, performs aggregations, and writes results back to Parquet partitioned by date.
processingSteps: 1. Read the 500GB Parquet dataset and confirm skew via df.rdd.getNumPartitions() and per-partition row counts.
2. Apply df.repartition(240) (3x the 80 cores) to round-robin redistribute into 240 evenly-sized ~2GB-then-balanced partitions.
3. Run the groupBy/aggregation transformations on the now-balanced data.
4. Before writing, coalesce(50) to reduce output file count without re-shuffling the balanced result.
5. Write the final aggregates to Parquet partitioned by event_date.
endToEndExample.output: Balanced aggregation output written as 50 Parquet files partitioned by date, computed within the SLA window with uniform task durations.
endToEndExample.monitoring: The Spark UI now shows near-uniform task durations in the aggregation stage and a single shuffle stage from the repartition with healthy shuffle read/write sizes and no large spills.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If executors had OOM'd on the original oversized partition, the repartition shrinks per-task memory; spill and OOM alerts are watched, and partition count is increased further if spills persist.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The job runtime drops from 90 minutes to 25 minutes because all 80 cores stay busy on equal work. The one-time repartition shuffle cost is far outweighed by eliminating straggler tasks, and the SLA is comfortably met.

industryUseCases.problem: Petabyte-scale ETL jobs suffered from skewed partitions where a few popular titles dominated event volume, causing straggler tasks.
industryUseCases.solution: Repartition data by a balanced key or round-robin before heavy aggregations, combined with AQE skew handling, to even out task load.
industryUseCases.benefits: Dramatically reduced job tail latency and cluster idle time, improving throughput and lowering compute cost for nightly pipelines.

industryUseCases.problem: Trip and event datasets were hash-partitioned by city, but a handful of large cities created severe partition skew during joins.
industryUseCases.solution: Repartition with salting on the skewed city key and tune partition counts to cluster cores so matching rows are co-located without overloading single partitions.
industryUseCases.benefits: Faster, more reliable joins with fewer OOM failures and predictable runtimes across their massive trip data lake.

industryUseCases.problem: Member-activity datasets read with too few partitions underutilized large clusters, leaving cores idle and slowing pipelines.
industryUseCases.solution: Increase parallelism by repartitioning input DataFrames to a multiple of total executor cores before wide transformations.
industryUseCases.benefits: Higher cluster utilization and shorter pipeline runtimes, enabling fresher analytics for member-facing features.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Repartition is the lever for matching parallelism to data growth: as datasets grow, increasing numPartitions keeps per-task memory bounded. However, the shuffle cost grows with data volume, so partition counts must be tuned against network and disk throughput rather than blindly increased.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Because shuffle outputs are persisted to local disk, Spark can recover individual failed reduce tasks by re-fetching shuffle blocks. Loss of an executor holding shuffle files, though, forces recomputation of the upstream map stage; external shuffle service mitigates this by serving blocks independent of executor lifecycle.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: In long-running or streaming contexts, enabling the external shuffle service and dynamic allocation keeps repartition shuffles resilient to executor churn, preserving availability of intermediate data across scale-up and scale-down events.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Repartition produces deterministic-count output but its shuffle is transient; recovery relies on re-reading source data and replaying the transformation. Idempotent writes (overwrite by partition) ensure that re-running a repartitioned job after failure yields consistent results.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Size partitions to ~100-200MB, set numPartitions to 2x-3x total cores, prefer coalesce when only reducing count, enable AQE to auto-coalesce post-shuffle partitions, and use salting or skew-join handling instead of naive hash repartition on skewed keys.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Eliminating stragglers via balanced repartition keeps the whole cluster busy, reducing wall-clock time and cost. Conversely, gratuitous repartitions add shuffle I/O cost, so each repartition should be justified by measurable downstream savings.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Repartition materializes intermediate data on local disk and transfers it over the network. For sensitive workloads, enable shuffle encryption (spark.io.encryption.enabled) and network encryption (spark.network.crypto.enabled) so shuffled data is protected at rest and in transit.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Use the Spark UI and event logs to track shuffle read/write bytes, spill to memory/disk, and task duration distribution. High variance in task time indicates remaining skew; large spills indicate undersized partition counts.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Repartition does not change data content (round-robin preserves all rows; hash preserves all rows per key), so row-count checks before and after should match exactly. This invariant is a useful validation step in pipelines.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log partition counts and per-stage shuffle metrics; alert on excessive spill, long task tails (skew), or shuffle fetch failures, which signal that repartition tuning or skew handling is needed.

recommendedPractices: **Right-size partitions:** Target ~100-200MB per partition and set numPartitions to roughly 2x-3x total executor cores.
**Prefer coalesce to reduce count:** Use coalesce instead of repartition when you only need fewer partitions without even sizing.
**Handle skew explicitly:** For skewed keys, use salting or AQE skew-join handling rather than plain repartition(col).
**Enable AQE:** Turn on spark.sql.adaptive.enabled so Spark can coalesce shuffle partitions automatically and reduce manual tuning.
engineeringStandards: Justify every repartition with a measured downstream benefit, since each one adds a full shuffle.
Validate row counts before and after repartition to confirm no data was lost or duplicated.
Avoid hardcoding very large partition counts; derive them from cluster size and data volume.
designRecommendations: Pre-partition by join key only when the same key is reused across multiple downstream joins/aggregations to amortize the shuffle.
Use repartitionByRange for ordered outputs or range-query-optimized writes.
Place repartition early enough to balance heavy stages but not so early that it shuffles data later filtered away.
namingConventions: Name balanced DataFrames descriptively, e.g., orders_balanced or events_repartitioned, to signal the layout change.
Document the chosen numPartitions and rationale (cores, data size) inline near the repartition call.
documentationStandards: Document why each repartition exists and the target partition size it aims for.
Record cluster core counts assumed by partition-count choices so they can be revisited when the cluster changes.
Note any skew-handling strategy (salting, AQE) applied alongside repartition.
testingStrategies: Test on representative skewed samples and inspect per-partition row counts to confirm balance.
Benchmark repartition vs coalesce for partition-reduction steps to pick the cheaper option.
Assert input and output row counts are equal to verify the transformation is non-destructive.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using repartition when coalesce would suffice to reduce partition count.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers reach for the more familiar repartition without realizing coalesce can reduce partitions without a shuffle.
commonMistakes.impact: Triggers an unnecessary full shuffle, adding network and disk I/O and lengthening the job for no balance benefit.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use coalesce(n) when only decreasing partition count and even sizing is not required; reserve repartition for increasing count or fixing skew.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hash-repartitioning on a heavily skewed key.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It seems logical to repartition(col) by the join/group key to co-locate rows.
commonMistakes.impact: All rows for a hot key land in one partition, recreating or worsening skew and producing straggler tasks despite the shuffle cost.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Detect key skew first; apply salting (append a random suffix to the key) or enable AQE skew-join handling instead of plain hash repartition.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing an arbitrary or excessively large partition count.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: A belief that more partitions always means more parallelism and speed.
commonMistakes.impact: Creates many tiny partitions, inflating task scheduling overhead and producing numerous small shuffle and output files.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Set numPartitions based on data size (~128MB/partition) and cluster cores (2x-3x total cores), and let AQE coalesce when possible.

comparisonSection.explanation: repartition always performs a full shuffle, moving all data over the network to produce evenly-sized partitions, and can increase or decrease the count. coalesce avoids a full shuffle by merging adjacent partitions on the same executors where possible, so it is far cheaper but can only reduce the count and may yield uneven partitions.

Round-robin repartition(n) ignores content and produces near-perfectly even partitions, ideal for fixing skew. Hash repartition(n, col) co-locates rows with the same key for joins/aggregations but inherits any skew present in the key distribution, so it can produce uneven partitions.

Only repartition can increase the number of partitions (coalesce cannot add partitions because it never shuffles). To decrease partitions cheaply, coalesce is preferred; to increase parallelism or evenly rebalance, repartition is required.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does repartition do in Spark?
beginnerQuestions.answer: repartition redistributes a DataFrame's data across a specified number of partitions by performing a full shuffle. repartition(n) round-robin distributes rows into n evenly-sized partitions, and repartition(n, col) hash-partitions by a column so same-key rows are co-located. It can both increase and decrease the partition count.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize the full shuffle and the two forms (numeric vs column). Mention it returns exactly the requested number of partitions.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you check the number of partitions of a DataFrame?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Use df.rdd.getNumPartitions(). You can also inspect per-partition distribution using spark_partition_id() in a groupBy to detect skew.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Show awareness of both the simple count and how to verify balance, which is the real reason you'd repartition.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between repartition and coalesce?
intermediateQuestions.answer: repartition performs a full shuffle and can increase or decrease partitions, producing evenly-sized partitions. coalesce avoids a full shuffle by merging adjacent partitions and can only decrease the count, which is cheaper but may produce uneven partitions and reduce upstream parallelism.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This is the most-asked repartition question. Stress shuffle vs no-shuffle, increase vs decrease, and even vs uneven outcomes.

intermediateQuestions.question: How would you use repartition to fix data skew?
intermediateQuestions.answer: If partitions are unevenly sized, repartition(n) round-robin redistributes rows into n balanced partitions, removing straggler tasks. If skew comes from a hot key during a join, plain hash repartition won't help; instead use salting or AQE skew-join handling.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Distinguish partition-size skew (round-robin fixes it) from key skew (needs salting/AQE), which interviewers probe for.

advancedQuestions.question: Why can repartition(col) make skew worse, and how do you mitigate it?
advancedQuestions.answer: repartition(col) uses a HashPartitioner, so all rows with the same key go to one partition. If a key is hot (e.g., one customer with millions of rows), that partition becomes huge, recreating skew. Mitigation includes salting the key with a random suffix to spread hot keys across partitions, or enabling AQE skew-join handling (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled) which splits skewed partitions automatically.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrates understanding that hashing preserves content distribution. Salting and AQE are the expected mitigations.

advancedQuestions.question: How does Adaptive Query Execution affect manual repartitioning decisions?
advancedQuestions.answer: AQE (Spark 3.0+) can coalesce post-shuffle partitions at runtime based on actual partition sizes (spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled) and split skewed partitions in joins. This reduces the need to manually tune spark.sql.shuffle.partitions or insert repartition calls, since Spark adapts partition counts using real statistics rather than static guesses.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Shows modern Spark knowledge: AQE automates much of what manual repartition used to do, though explicit repartition is still needed to increase parallelism or pre-partition by key.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your Spark job reads a Parquet dataset into 8 partitions, but one task runs 10x longer than the rest and the cluster of 100 cores is mostly idle. How do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The long task plus idle cluster signals skew and under-parallelism. First confirm with per-partition row counts. The fix is to round-robin repartition into a count matched to cores to both balance and parallelize. Verify with the UI that task durations even out.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Confirm skew via spark_partition_id() counts, then df.repartition(200) (~2x the 100 cores) to round-robin balance and increase parallelism. Verify uniform task durations in the Spark UI. If skew stems from a hot join key, additionally apply salting or AQE skew handling.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a daily Spark pipeline that joins a large skewed orders table with a customer dimension and writes partitioned Parquet output. Address partitioning strategy.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Read both tables; detect skew on customer_id. For the join, rely on AQE skew-join handling or salt the skewed keys rather than naive hash repartition. After aggregation, coalesce to a reasonable file count before writing partitioned by date. Use repartition only to set parallelism (2x-3x cores) on heavy stages.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Hash repartition by join key reduces join shuffle but risks key skew; round-robin balances but doesn't co-locate keys. Coalesce before write avoids a shuffle but can be uneven; repartition before write gives even files at shuffle cost.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Scale numPartitions with data volume to keep partitions ~128MB. Enable AQE for adaptive partition coalescing and skew splitting. Use the external shuffle service and dynamic allocation so shuffles survive executor churn as the cluster scales.

followUpQuestions: What is the default value of spark.sql.shuffle.partitions and how does it relate to repartition?
Can coalesce ever increase the number of partitions?
What is repartitionByRange and when would you use it?
How does salting help when repartitioning by a skewed key?
What metrics in the Spark UI tell you a repartition was needed or successful?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: repartition redistributes data into an exact number of partitions via a full shuffle, round-robin for even sizing or hash by column to co-locate keys.
keyConcepts: Full shuffle: always triggered, the dominant cost.
repartition(n): round-robin, even partitions, fixes skew.
repartition(n, col): hash partitioning, co-locates keys.
Can increase or decrease partition count.
Coalesce is cheaper for reducing count only.
formulas: target_partition = hash(key) % numPartitions  (for repartition by column)
interviewPoints: Only repartition can increase partition count.
Round-robin fixes size skew; hash can cause key skew.
Use salting or AQE for skewed keys.
Size partitions ~128MB and to cluster cores.
quickNotes: repartition(n) is round-robin and content-agnostic, giving even partitions.
repartition(n, col) uses a HashPartitioner; skewed keys reintroduce skew.
Always justify a repartition by a measurable downstream gain since it costs a full shuffle.
Enable AQE to auto-coalesce shuffle partitions and split skewed ones.
Row counts must be identical before and after a repartition (non-destructive).

keyTakeaways: repartition always performs a full shuffle to produce exactly the requested number of partitions, and is the only option that can increase partition count.
repartition(n) round-robin distributes rows for even sizing (the canonical skew fix), while repartition(n, col) hash-partitions to co-locate same-key rows for joins and aggregations.
Hash repartitioning on a skewed key recreates skew; use salting or AQE skew-join handling instead.
Prefer coalesce over repartition when you only need to reduce partition count without even sizing, to avoid an unnecessary shuffle.
Right-size partitions to ~128MB and set numPartitions to roughly 2x-3x total cores, and enable AQE to automate much of the tuning.
